utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, can we have the case called, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin. Are you hearing me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Brdjanin. General Talic, I don't know if you speak English, but are you hearing me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you too. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner together for the first time with Julian Nicholls, another member of the team, who is here this morning to protect me from Defence counsel. And as usual, Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner and good morning to the whole team. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm sorry that I had so intimidated the Prosecutor. I'm John Ackerman. I appear with Milka Maglov and Tania Radosavljevic for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. And appearances for General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. I am Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic and I'm assisted by Maitre Fabien Masson. I'm representing General Talic. I would also like to apologise to the Chamber on behalf of Maitre de Roux who is absent today and will be absent the following week too, because of medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. And good morning to you as well. So preliminaries. Regarding the schedule of sittings right through the end of July, I have gone through it, I have not discussed it as yet with the other two judges mainly because I wanted to check one thing, also because I had made arrangements accordingly that when we met and discussed the schedule for the first three or -- for the first months, anyway, in particular with regard to the Easter period. I have a recollection that we had agreed that we will stop from the 22nd and recommence on the 4th of April. That's what I remember. I have asked Ms. Thompson to check it out for me and I'll come back to you after that because it's not just me who has that recollection but also my two colleagues. So we will come back to you later on after the break on that. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you're probably right about that. I intended to look at that piece of transcript and just forgot. I didn't remember what date we were supposed to recommence and I got in a hurry and just forgot to look.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: My recollection was -- I'm sorry, I managed to do my back in slightly, but my recollection was that it was the 2nd of April because we had a discussion about April Fool's Day, so it was the Tuesday immediately following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not contesting that. I'm just -- I just want to find out, that's all. Ms. Thompson will dig it up. So the other thing -- yes, my microphone is on. I think you wanted to mike submissions on the procedural point that you briefly hinted at at the end of yesterday's sitting, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're speaking about the journalist situation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly because it's something that I asked you to mention so that we would more or less come prepared for it this morning and then we can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if we could have the argument in private session? I know that because it's press, there has been interest in it. There are a number of reasons why the second journalist involved has certain concerns and unless anybody -- Mr. Ackerman objects, I think it would be helpful if we just hold this discussion in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm fundamentally opposed to non-public proceedings in an International Court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me suggest something before you continue. Can we go into private session now for a few minutes until Ms. Korner tells us or rather expands on what she has just said? That may be enough to convince you to go or to continue in private session after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It may be and that would be fine, Your Honour, if you want to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objections because I think that it doesn't concern me, or rather that it doesn't concern my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but it concerns the whole process actually because we could come across other similar instances later on where you would have an interest. So I --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as the private session is concerned, I am opposed to it as Mr. Ackerman is, but in this case, I can't express a position because Ms. Korner said that this part did not concern my client in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go into private session for a few minutes first and then depending on what you ever to say, Ms. Korner, we will decide whether to continue it in private session for a while or whether to go public once more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Ackerman, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My position was stated to some extent yesterday. I'll call that position number 1. And that is, that the date of these interviews is in March of 1993, which is well beyond the time of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: January, January.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, January, 1993. It's beyond the term of the indictment and I think therefore irrelevant. It's fairly clear that the subject matter of the interview was Mr. Brdjanin as a minister of the government was being asked his views regarding the cantonisation plan put forward by Vance and Owen and at that point, all parties were seeking to -- it appeared that the Vance-Owen Plan was going to basically freeze the situation as it existed, that there would be a Serbian canton, a Croat canton, and a Muslim canton. And so that's what he was being asked to comment upon, his views regarding that process, which I think lends no -- sheds no light whatsoever on the events of 1992. It was a political situation of the moment that is not relevant to any of the issues in this case. Argument number 2, and this is situational because we are only in one spot at this point and the spot we are in is with regard to (redacted) --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Didn't you yourself suggest that you would be saying, Mr. Ackerman, instead?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you've not commented on my age recently, perhaps you should. I don't know what to do at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please have it redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: X1, Witness 1. Witness 1 was not able to have a conversation with Mr. Brdjanin because he does not speak his language, and so he was totally dependent upon what someone else told him that Mr. Brdjanin was saying. And it seems to me, if we are interested in the best evidence, then if anyone is going to come to give evidence about that conversation, it should be the person who actually was speaking the same language as Mr. Brdjanin and heard the exact words of Mr. Brdjanin. So I think that fairly well states my position in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution say this: The interview itself took place just outside the period of the indictment, we accept that. But so close to it that we say that the words used by Brdjanin are indicative and which one can see when taken with the other evidence in this case, of his intention in respect of what the Prosecution say was the ultimate aim of this whole campaign, namely the expulsion, the forcible expulsion of non-Serbs from the territories known as the ARK. Your Honours, the fact that those words were uttered at a time outside the period which you are concerned with, we say is irrelevant because we say that Your Honours are entitled to infer from what was said in January, 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To all intents and purposes the alleged words could have been said just yesterday and they would still be relevant to the events of ten years ago. So that point you needn't elaborate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's our position. Your Honour, the second matter is a much more complex matter really in one sense. Mr. -- now I'm doing it and that's why I asked for private session. It is impossible. The witness made a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He signed an acknowledgement to attend. The second man hasn't made a statement. I appreciate that, as I said before, that the first man doesn't speak the language and was relying on the second person to interpret. But as I think I said earlier, it's no different from effectively an investigator seeing a witness and taking a statement through an interpreter. Your Honour, the weight of course Your Honours will perhaps take into account the fact that this wasn't directly said to him. Your Honours, that in a sense is a subsidiary matter, although as I say, the first man has a -- or his ex-employers have instructed counsel to argue the matter. It was due for hearing on Monday but because there are still these matters outstanding, I think Your Honours agreed that it could be put back and I so informed counsel for the first witness. It may be that at the moment all that Your Honours are required to do is to give a ruling first of all whether or not the conversations or the interview is in itself admissible. The matter of how it then comes before the Court is something I believe that Mr. Ackerman and myself may still be able to discuss and perhaps arrive at some agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will just give you very briefly my first thoughts. Then with the understanding that I will discuss it with the other two judges, unless I have an indication that there is agreement straight away. If we need to discuss it further, we will discuss it further and come back to you. But what I think should be the approach -- I notice that there are some parts in the witness's statement, although I acknowledge that this is not an exhibit as yet, but this is why I always ask to be handed copies of the witness statements before, because that would put me in a better position to take certain decisions. At the end, at the very end of this witness statement, Witness 1 says, "I am willing to speak with investigators for the Tribunal, but I hesitate as a journalist to testify before the Court. I would prefer that my statement and article stand for themselves. However, if that were not possible, I would be willing to testify, that the quotes accredited to Brdjanin are true and accurate." And I would take this as the starting point, very starting point, because I have the prospects of a witness coming here in this courtroom in a position whereby he can follow-up and confirm this statement that he has made in the written statement he gave to the Prosecution. In other words, that he is telling us that he is in a position not only to testify, if he is constrained to, he wouldn't like to, but if he finds himself with his back to the wall and he needs to testify, then he is in a position to confirm to us that the quotes accredited to Brdjanin are true and accurate. So that's point one 1. Point number 2, if you look at the centre of the first page of the statement, where he describes the interview he and Witness 2 had with Brdjanin, he is not exactly giving a picture or describing an event as if he were just a passive observer, not understanding what was happening. In other words, as I understand it, as I take it, there were three men involved in this interview, your client, Mr. Ackerman, as it is alleged here, and Witness 1 and Witness 2. It was Witness 2 who was being proactive in the sense. It was Witness 2 who knew the language and was conducting the interview. But Witness 1, who presumably, as I take it, did not understand the language, says, throughout the interview, Brdjanin seemed very self-assured. We didn't have to work hard to obtain from him. In retrospect, I think Brdjanin was indicating to us that he was not yet totally in command of the expulsion policy because he talked about how he would do things if he were in charge. And he goes on and on and on. This is not a man, a witness, who has just been a passive observer depending exclusively for Witness 2 to draw up some or more conclusions. It seems to me that we have a witness who at least to an extent can give us some information. Third point I wanted to make was that I fully understand that if Witness 2 is not brought forward to give evidence in private, in closed or whatever kind of session, then it may well end up with us having a situation whereby we would have heard Witness 1, taken stock of his perhaps witness statement to an extent, and come to the conclusion that the article as such, given the circumstances of this being basically and essentially a hearsay evidence par excellence, does not reach that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. standard which has been accepted and applied by this Tribunal in the past for the -- for giving weight, probative weight to that particular document. In other words, remembering or reminding you that what is important for this Chamber is not whether the document itself ought to be admitted in evidence or not. Rather, it is the probative value that it can receive that is important. We may end up in a situation whereby we would have heard Witness 1 but come to the conclusion that for all intense and purposes, his evidence is not going to be of any importance to us. But I would still think that we ought to go ahead with Witness 1 and I would suggest at this point in time just to put Witness 1 in the utmost liberty, make him feel comfortable in giving evidence, to offer some kind of, I don't know whether we go into private session or some sort of -- to make sure, in other words, that Witness 2 is not mentioned in the course of his evidence, if necessary, especially if that person is, as you put it, Ms. Korner, possibly in danger. The Trial Chamber has every interest in protecting him. And on that score, perhaps we could also entice Witness 2 to come forward and testify if he knows that his evidence will be given in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, neither witness -- well, Witness 1, I think it's more a situation of his ex-employers. The American press takes a very strong line, and I understand in the United States has a certain amount of protection from testifying, which is certainly not available in England and Wales. I think it's the principle of whether the journalist should be testifying that both of them are urging although, as I say, Witness 2 has severe concerns, personal concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't make a suggestion to you obviously because I don't think you need suggestions from the Trial Chamber, Ms. Korner, you're experienced enough. But I do seriously think that maybe the case of considering, affording him some kind of protective measure before he gives evidence because this is serious business. I mean, in my country more or less the situation is very similar to yours. We would not be in -- strictly speaking, there is no such thing as a privilege attached to the professional journalist, and theoretically speaking, if a journalist in giving evidence refuses to give certain information, technically speaking, he or she could be subject to -- but we never resort to that. More or less we try each -- I have tried it in my -- the whole time -- my whole career, to protect the journalist as much as I could, respecting the confidentiality that he has a right to, even if it may not be a legal right, not to disclose his source of information and other information. It is important. I think it is important. And more or less, since we do not have a rule here, I would say that the Trial Chamber would be more or less rather tend to protecting rather than exposing the witness to any possible prejudice or danger, especially physical danger. So I would suggest to you to consider, seriously consider what I have stated, and I'm sure -- I think more or less, I mean although I was saying what I personally think with the reservation that I will discuss later, I think -- I take it that more or less we are on the same wavelength and we can go along on those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful for those indications. Can I take it that Your Honour is ruling that this interview is admissible? Because that's the argument that was raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The argument -- Ms. Korner, when I have a witness who has previously confirmed to you that he is in a position to testify if asked to and forced to, testify that the quotes accredited to Brdjanin are true and accurate, how can I refuse to admit it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the argument from Mr. Ackerman was because it was outside the indictment period it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, that is, as I'm trying to explain, if in the course of the evidence it transpires that what was stated to Witness 2 and Witness 1 outside the period of the indictment refers exclusively to events outside the period of the indictment, and do not shed a light, throw a light on the events preceding the dates of the interview, or related to the events falling within the time frame of the indictment, then obviously I'm going to stop the witness and say, "We don't need you any more." But as it is, even on the face of it, I think -- I think that the evidence could throw a light on the possible frame of mind that the accused may have had in 1992, April to December. If that is not the case, obviously I'm going to throw this witness out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's as simple as that. I cannot a priori exclude because he stated something in 1993 it necessarily couldn't be relevant to the events happening in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well then, Your Honour, I see Mr. Ackerman is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to say that since you have made your ruling regarding relevance that I really have no further argument to make regarding this matter, because what I cannot do and will not do is try to interfere with the Prosecution's right to call relevant evidence of any kind that they want to call. So I think it now becomes a matter between the Trial Chamber and the Prosecutor as to securing the attendance of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And that's up to you, Ms. Korner, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I was hoping to be able to have a further discussion with Mr. Ackerman, but if it's unfruitful, if it's not fruitful, then I will make arrangements. As I say, the witness should have been here on Monday to answer, but counsel couldn't make that day and suggested Wednesday of next week but because it was still up in the air may we come back to Your Honour about a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't saying that I wouldn't discuss the matter with Ms. Korner. What I was saying was that it is not appropriate for me to argue to the Chamber that relevant evidence ought not be called if the Prosecution can call it. That's all I was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the other thing -- yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just mention two matters? Administratively? Firstly, the humanitarian organisation has now considered Your Honour's ruling, the statement will be disclosed. We are just getting them together today. However, I'm told that having told the Chamber that we would like to call them immediately after the Easter break, one of the witnesses will not be available. He will be away. And so we will have to make arrangements so we won't seek to call them immediately then. Secondly, I forgot yesterday, I'm afraid, and I hope that the slight delay won't matter to say the witnesses for next week. I know we are supposed to say Thursday but I keep forgetting. Your Honours, the witnesses will be 7.175. Your Honours already have the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 7.158. Your Honours will be given the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically we are skipping 7.197 for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We are going to, can we say, 7.197 almost certainly will not be called at all because we consider that his evidence has already been covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, I'm not sure, my feeling is that 7.158, who rather like the present witness is a very document heavy one will probably take the rest of the week but in case we have also got 7.152 and 7.42. The -- all of these witnesses, Your Honour, require -- are protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. Yes. Okay. So there is another preliminary issue that arises from yesterday's sitting. Those three documents, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What the Trial Chamber requires from you is some kind of a reliable affirmation that those -- regarding the source of those three documents tending to prove that there is some indicia of reliability.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. Your Honour, while we are on that subject, I need to ask the Chamber your views regarding a matter of evidence and procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am accustomed, both in the United States and in my practice before this Tribunal in a prior case, to a procedure whereby it was -- it would be permissible for me to confront a witness with a document that had not been disclosed to the Prosecution if my only purpose in doing so was for the purpose of impeachment of the witness. In other words, if I'm not offering the document for the truth of its contents, but only for the limited purpose of what light it might throw upon the credibility of the witness, then it doesn't come within the reciprocal disclosure rule and the rules of this Tribunal. And I would ask the Chamber to agree with me that that is the case and that if I do not want to offer a document for the truth of its contents but only to attack the credibility of a witness, then I'm not required to disclose it to the Prosecutor in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, Mr. Ackerman, I know it's only 20 to 10.00 but we are all very much fully awake already, but what was the purpose of these three documents? The purpose of bringing forward these three documents, as I understood it, was to prove that when the witness stated yesterday or the day before that no Serb was ever prosecuted for having failed to respond to the mobilisation, call for mobilisation, he was not saying the truth. And you were purporting to prove him wrong, or to prove that he was saying a lie, telling a lie, by bringing forward three documents tending to prove that three Serbs had been prosecuted. So basically, how can you argue now that you are not trying to prove the truth or the contents of these three documents? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Very simple, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can only prove that the witness was not telling us the truth if what is contained in those three documents actually means that there were charges brought against three Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very simple. I would say to you that you cannot consider the content of those three documents as an offer of proof by me that three Serbs were actually prosecuted. I can bring witnesses to prove that, and I will probably will do that. The only purpose of using a document like that, if you're doing it strictly for impeachment purposes is to give the witness an opportunity to say whether he changes his position based upon seeing the documents. If he says, yes, fine, if he says no, fine. But it deals with his credibility, not with proof of the contents of the documents. I have just been informed that that was also the rule that was applied in the Srebrenica case, that a document did not have to be disclosed if it was used only for impeachment purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But there you may have a point in certain instances. You may have a point in certain instances. But in this particular case that we are dealing with, this is certainly not the case because the purpose of using these three documents was, as I have just explained to you, that you are confronting the witness with three documents in which you state to him that three persons with Yugoslav names were charged with having failed -- with Serb names, were charged with having failed to respond to the call for mobilisation. In other words, that they were charged, as against what he had stated earlier, namely that to his knowledge, no Serb was ever prosecuted for this offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm saying to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically how can you avoid bringing, discussing with the witness at least the contents of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely you should never put the Prosecution in a position whereby they are taken by surprise and they are not in a position to -- this is not a case of you having the birth certificate of the witness who comes here and says, I was born on the 18th of March of 1940, and you know that he was not born on the 18th March of 1940. It is not a case of a witness coming forward and saying, "I never had a passport," and you have a photocopy of his passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've made my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you tell him, "This is your birth certificate. This is your passport." This is something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've made my point for the record, and as always, I will respect your rulings. I always will. With regard to the source of these three documents, what I can tell you right now, Your Honours, is the following. I sent an e-mail message to one of my investigators in Banja Luka immediately after court yesterday, saying, "I need to know where you got the documents showing criminal charges filed against Serbs who failed to respond to the mobilisation. I must advise the Chamber in the morning." The response reads: "I got them from OMO, [No interpretation]. They used to be called [No interpretation]. I have the approval from the Minister of Defence. That's the response." And if necessary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure what -- maybe the interpreters can tell you what [No interpretation] translates to. I think it's the Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A department of the Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A department of the Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can bring this particular investigator to testify, if the Chamber wants me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, are you happy with that, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two matters that arise from this. First of all, if Mr. Ackerman is saying that he's not putting forward these documents for the truth of their contents, then they are completely irrelevant. They don't get admitted at all and all that -- if he doesn't know whether they are true or not, he intends to call evidence at a later stage to prove either the authenticity or the truth of the contents, or live evidence from Serbs, then the proper way of putting things is to put to the witness, "You're wrong or you're not telling the truths," however they feel about it, and not try to put in documents which he says he has no idea whether the contents are true. That's the first matter. The second matter is this: Under Rule 67(C), Mr. Ackerman, having invoked the provisions of Rule 66(B), that is reciprocal disclosure, the Rule 67(C) states the Prosecutor shall be entitled to inspect any books, documents, photographs and tangible objects which are within the custody or control of the Defence and which it intends to use as evidence at the trial. At the moment, the excuse being used is, "I don't know what I intend to use as evidence." That may or may not be right in respect of some documents, but we submit that clearly, where documents are intended to be used, because it's clear in advance that the witness is going to say something like this, then we are entitled to see these documents in advance and not just produced on the day when they are intended to be used. Your Honour, with respect to whether or not what Mr. Ackerman has just said is sufficient to establish the source, Your Honour, for the moment, I'm not proposing to pursue that matter any further until I can take some instructions about this. But our submission would be simply that these documents, if Mr. Ackerman doesn't know whether they are true or not, are not being put forward for the truth of their contents, but merely to in some way impeach the witness, that does not in itself make them admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't accept Mr. Ackerman saying that these are not being put forward in a way you have just described it because basically if you look at these documents and the fifth line after the name of the person charged, you have, "By ethnicity, Serb, citizen of SFRY." So basically, the whole -- the importance of these three documents lies in that word, and the fact that he was trying to make use of these three documents to contradict or prove the witness wrong in stating that no Serb was ever prosecuted for this crime or for this offence because I'm not quite sure whether it was a crime or an offence, I see that there is some kind of a difference in treatment the way it was conceived, but any way --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, at the moment, the situation is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think they can be admitted for the moment and then we see afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Except that can I just remind Your Honour the evidence from the witnesses -- these aren't charges. These are reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I've taken that into consideration already. Definitely. And from the face of these documents, on the face of it, each document does not purport to be a real charge. I mean, I don't know what it is, I have never seen anything like it in my life. But any way, perhaps you would be in a position to enlighten us later on by means of some other kind of evidence or other kind of witness, Mr. Ackerman, what these documents are because that -- the importance or relevance of these documents could well arise at some future point in time, when we have a clearer picture because until now I don't have a clear picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fully believe there will come a stage in this case when I will be able to put on evidence that a number of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Serbs were in fact charged with offences for failure to respond to the mobilisation, a number of Serbs were fired from their positions in various industries for failure to respond to mobilisation. I think I can -- I will bring evidence to prove all those things. I'm disturbed a bit by Ms. Korner's comment that I should not be offering documents as evidence if I think they are not true. I haven't suggested to you that I think these are not true. I's in the same position she is. She has thousands of documents she has no idea whether they are true or not. They were taken from various places in search and seizure. Some of them have no signatures or stamps. She can't you that those are true. She can't tell you that the contents are true. She has no idea. And it is true of all of us. We all gather up documents where we gather up documents. We don't know if they are true or not. What I'm saying to you, and not specifically with regard to these documents, all I'm saying to you is that it is the law where I am used to practising, and in at least two cases that I know of in this Tribunal, that if you want to impeach a witness with a document, and you're offering it solely for impeachment purposes, not for the truth of its contents, then it does not need to be disclosed. And Rule 67(C) which the Prosecutor refers to makes it fairly clear that you have to disclose that which you intend to use as evidence at the trial. In other words, evidence that you're offering for the truth of its contents. That's my position. And I understand the Court's ruling and I am not arguing that these particular documents should fall into that category. And I have given today the Prosecutor a large number of documents that I received just yesterday. They haven't been translated yet. I am just passingly familiar with what they say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau is smiling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suspect I will use them in some way but I don't know. But I've given them to them as she requested I do yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do follow the practice that I suggested to you yesterday. I fully understand that there may be instances where you honestly don't know whether you would be making use of a document or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you wait and then decide at the very last moment that you're going to make use of that document, and come here and surprise not just us, the three judges here, because we would be surprised too, but your colleague on the other side, who has every interest in the case as much as you have, and every right, and who I understand have not been withholding any information from you and have fully honoured their commitments and their obligations under the Statute and under the Rules as far as disclosure is concerned, then I have to protect the Prosecution. Just as much as I would protect the Defence if they did the same thing to you. All I asked was you had them a day before, two days before, you could have given these documents to Ms. Korner saying, "Probably I will be making use of these. I'm sorry I don't have them translated. These purportedly are such and such a thing." And that would have saved us a good hour easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We discussed that yesterday, Your Honour, and I accepted your position on it and this morning I handed her documents that arrived just yesterday that I haven't translated. So I'm doing what you have suggested that I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this morning I wanted to try to suggest to you that there were situations where I didn't have to disclose documents if I was going to use them for impeachment only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There may be such situations yes, I agree with you. There may be such situations, but certainly I don't see these three documents falling within that particular category that you tried to suggest this morning, because first question to the witness was, "You see these documents?"

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want them in that category. I'm offering them for their contents, not as impeachment and you've accepted them that way so I'm not arguing about these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's a complete reversal. I understood one moment ago these were being put in for impeaching the witness. Now we're --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's just not true. When I stood up I said to you I want to raise a matter regarding the Rules of Evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But why should you raise a matter regarding a Rule of Evidence that is not before us at all? I mean, if you're talking about three documents which you are presenting or bringing forward as a proof of the truth of the contents, why should you argue with regard to another rule or practice or decision or procedural rule of this Trial Chamber that has got nothing to do with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is very simple. I may have a document in my possession right now that I may want to use for impeachment of the next witness that is coming up, not for the truth of the contents but just to impeach that witness. I know that if I give that document to the Prosecutor, they will then give it to the witness and the witness will have a chance to concoct some story that explains it which he wouldn't be able --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate you're trying to save the Trial Chamber a lot of time. Thank you Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know why this has turned into a major argument but, Your Honour, I strongly dispute Mr. Ackerman's reading of Rule 67(C). I'm assisted by my own American expert who is sitting to my left this morning. I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe he's from Texas

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that it is a rule in the United States that there is a difference between documents used to impeach a witness and documents which are then put in, but Mr. Ackerman is asking for these documents to be made exhibits. If that's not evidence, what is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, any documents that Mr. Ackerman seeks to put in as exhibits or indeed I would -- and certainly as exhibits, are evidence, to use as evidence, and he must comply, in our submission, with Rule 67(C). Now, as to whether there is a difference between putting a document before a witness and saying, "I want to you read this document. Do not tell us what the contents are. Having read that document, do you still wish to adhere to the answer that you gave or the evidence that you gave?" If the answer is, "Yes, I do," then that's the end of the matter. Those documents don't go in. They are not evidence. Your Honours don't even hear what the document is. Indeed I suppose on that basis we don't hear. But if a document is to be put before a witness, Your Honours are to be given copies, then that document is being put in as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can close the matter here and proceed, Mr. Ackerman. These three documents are being admitted as exhibits and we move from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree almost completely with what Ms. Korner just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You couldn't but agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With the possible exception, with this exception. It would be improper for me to put a document to the witness for impeachment purposes and also keep it from the Prosecutor. I think I would have to disclose it to the Prosecutor at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. But beyond that, I agree with her. It shouldn't go into evidence if I'm not offering it into evidence. And I think that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. That stands to reason. So can we call the witness in? Please admit the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, Mr. Dzonlic. Sorry to have kept you waiting but we had some very heated arguments on procedural matters before you came in not having to do anything with you. You will be now asked to make the usual statement promising to say the truth, to tell us the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Then you may sit down and we will continue with the cross-examination. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down. Good morning to you, once more. Mr. Ackerman you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you start, do we need to provide the witness with any documents that you are going to refer to beforehand so that we don't waste time each time we need a document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's identify those straight away and have them handed to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I hope I can get them all. BD31, P227, P470. There is a document, disclosure 3.111, which is Official Gazette Banja Luka number 11, which I might refer to, might not. P295, P43, P153.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ackerman, before you continue, the Trial Chamber has taken the liberty, at least with the Prosecution, and I thought it was something known to everyone, that before a witness is going to give evidence, more or less we try to ask for information as to which documents will be made use or reference will be made to in the course of the testimony. The Prosecution has been cooperative in that regard. More or less before Mr. Dzonlic was coming over, we knew that he was going to be asked or these documents will be made use of in the course of the evidence. If you could adopt -- you and of course the Defence team for General Talic, the same system. I understand that you may have to increase or decrease or vary the lists as we go along in the course of the examination-in-chief, but if before, say, a day or two before you start your cross-examination, you let us know which documents we need to have before us, you would be helping the Trial Chamber a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd be happy to do that to the extent that I'm capable of doing it, Your Honour. There is no reason for me to try to hide anything from anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not an imposition. It's a suggestion that the Trial Chamber makes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think maybe with only one or two exceptions these are all documents that the witness was referring to yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, I don't agree with you at all. More than half of the documents have not been asked upon in the course of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Probably are. You usually are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually they say that I only was wrong once and that's when I said I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You thought you were wrong and you weren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzonlic.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that you didn't personally know Mr. Brdjanin on the first day you testified here, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that he was in the republican assembly from the Banja Luka region?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you say Banja Luka region, do you mean Banja Luka municipality?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the region of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How -- I've not heard that term before. What is the region of Banja Luka? Is that more than the opstina?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It covers several municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that the Autonomous Region of Krajina? Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not talking about that. I know that there was a region and I know that he came from the Banja Luka region. I wasn't referring to the Autonomous Krajina when I used that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Does that region have its own government of some kind?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where is it defined as a region? How -- is it some formal, legal concept or is it just an informal thing or what is it? We've not heard that before here. So you could help us, I think.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina was divided up into regions, not officially by law but there was the Bihac region, the Banja Luka region, the Tuzla basin, the Sarajevo region. And that is what I was referring to. Territorially in general terms, and not as a legally defined term.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you seen a map that shows these regions?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So they are not formal in the sense that they have been drawn on maps or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was customary to refer to the Tuzla basin region, the Bihac region, the Banja Luka region, which covered Banja Luka and a couple of surrounding municipalities which were by their industry and economically linked together. And that is what I meant when I said from the Banja Luka region area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Should we -- maybe you can help us with this. Should we take it from your testimony that people were elected to the assembly from these regions, like Mr. Brdjanin was elected to represent the Banja Luka region in the assembly?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. People were elected by municipalities, on municipality lists. Only I don't know on which municipality list he was, but I do know that he came from the region of Banja Luka and later, I learnt that he came from the Celinac municipality which is in the immediate vicinity of Banja Luka. So when I use the term "region," I meant that he came from Banja Luka or the surrounding area. However, the election lists were drawn up for each municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So are you saying that you now know that Mr. Brdjanin represented the Celinac municipality in the republican assembly?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, not now, but then in 1991 and 1992, I didn't know that he was from Celinac. I didn't even know that he was from Banja Luka. I wasn't sure on which list his name figured but I later learnt that he was from the Celinac municipality, and as far as I know to this day, he is from Celinac municipality, though I never saw any documents showing where he was born, where he lived, or where he resided, which was -- you had to be registered in a particular municipality for at least six months to be able to appear on the list of candidates, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me -- I must have asked that question very inartfully. What I was trying to ask you was, do you now know that during the time you're testifying about, that late 1991, early 1992, that Mr. Brdjanin was in the republican assembly as a representative of the Celinac municipality?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you also told us that if you were a representative from a particular municipality, then you were required, to the extent possible, to attend the municipal assembly meetings of that municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so Mr. Brdjanin, as a representative from Celinac would have been required to attend the municipal assembly meetings in Celinac; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You also told us that you thought he was on the candidates list in Banja Luka for the elections, multi-party elections in 1990 and let me ask that you take a look at Exhibit BD31, and tell me first of all if you recognise what it is.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you see the list of candidates for the SDS?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That list has, I think, 130 names on it. Do you see Mr. Brdjanin's name on that list?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that you heard Mr. Brdjanin make certain statements on the radio in 1991 and 1992, statements about Muslim people, about the numbers who should remain in the Banja Luka region. You're familiar with the statements I'm referring to, are you not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you like to change your testimony about that and agree with me that, first of all, you didn't hear those statements but were simply told that he had made such statements?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't like to change my testimony, and I cannot agree with you that I heard it from someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you like to change your testimony and agree with me that it was only in 1993 that you heard or someone told you they had heard Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Brdjanin say certain things on the radio?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say -- when I said I heard him, I didn't say that he said such and such a thing in 1992, and in 1993 something else. When I was speaking, I think we were talking about what he said in 1991, and in 1992 and 1993, as far as I can remember, in the statement I made. When I said in 1991 he said there should be a plebiscite of the Serb people and a Serb state should be formed and Yugoslavia -- that a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina should belong to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you agree or disagree with the following statement: "He was very frequently on the radio, TV, and in the newspapers, especially in 1993. Before that, he was obviously not considered respectable as a spokesperson of the SDS. In 1991 and 1992, he was rarely interviewed." Do you agree or disagree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know as to what you're saying, that he was a spokesman. Whether it was frequently or infrequently is something again that I cannot comment on, but I do know that I personally heard him on the media, the radio, and some statements in the local newspaper Glas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So is it your testimony, then, that you disagree with that statement that I just read to you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you read it out to me once again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I will. Referring to Mr. Brdjanin, "He was very frequently on the radio, TV and in newspapers, especially in 1993. Before that, he was obviously not considered respectable as a spokesperson of the SDS. In 1991 and 1992, he was rarely interviewed."

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding 1993, I can't know because I left on the 26th of February, 1993, so at the beginning of the year. But let me say again, whether it was frequently or infrequently is something I can't say, and I don't know what that means, "frequently or not." But I personally did hear him. As for this statement you read out, it's something I don't know what to say about. I don't know what is meant by "frequently or not frequently" being interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How about just the statement, "In 1991 and 1992, he was rarely interviewed"? Would you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I can't say that I agree or disagree, because I'm not qualified to speak about the media. All I can say is that I personally heard him on the media. Not once but several times, I heard him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So can I take it that your answer is that you don't know if that statement is true or not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Who did you meet with about your testimony that you were going to give here before you actually came into the Trial Chamber and started testifying? Who did you discuss your testimony with before coming into the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With no one. I didn't discuss my testimony with anyone before entering the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You never had any meetings with the Prosecutor about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had talks concerning my statement and certain corrections in that statement. I was given my statement to read through. I don't consider that to be a meeting in the sense that you asked me. I had made several statements previously, and when I came here, I was given the statement to read out again. If you're referring to that meeting, then, yes, I did have that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you have any conversation of any kind, whether it was a meeting, a telephone, correspondence, any form of communication, about the subject of your testimony with any person other than a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor prior to coming here and giving your testimony?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just communicated with my parents, to let them know that I was coming here. No, I didn't have any communication with anyone concerning my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you not have meetings with some people from the AID office?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't meet with them. They drove me to the airport in an official car, from my home to the airport, but I didn't have a meeting with them of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How long a drive would that have been?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I waited in front of my building from 1.15. They were due to come at 1.30. I was ready at 1.15 waiting. They were a bit late, maybe five or ten minutes. There was a van, and there were other people inside, and they apologised because they needed to transport these other witnesses who were coming to testify, and the trip to the airport took about half an hour, half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you had no discussion with the AID people or any of these other witnesses about the testimony you were coming here to give?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said we were going to The Hague. It was known that we were going to The Hague, that those people were going to The Hague too, but we didn't discuss our testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want to change subjects now. I want to go to the issue of the mobilisation. You told us in your direct testimony that you represented some people with respect to mobilisation orders that they had received, correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you told us that you had been instructed by your clients to pursue this matter I think your words were, up to -- "up to some international court." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What international court did you tell these clients in 1992 had the competence to hear their issues regarding mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say anything to them about that. There was the Court in Strasbourg for human rights violations and they said that their rights were in jeopardy and they themselves said that they would like this to be taken right up to the level of international courts. But I didn't tell them which particular courts I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you contend that there was an international [Realtime transcript read in error "small"] court that would have jurisdiction over the mobilisation orders in 1992 in former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not just cases of mobilisation. There were cases regarding employment and property rights, and mostly those people who were saying that they would like to take those cases to international courts, they were people that had such property complaints and complaints regarding employment and not in connection with mobilisation, for which they would address international courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the transcript has rendered my question to be contended that there was a "small court"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what I'd asked him was, "Do you contend that there was an international court"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have to ask the question again because I don't think it was answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcript contains an obvious mistake. You certainly did not ask the witness whether he contends there was a small court, but you asked him whether he contends there was an international court that would have jurisdiction over the mobilisation orders in 1992 in former Yugoslavia. So I think with my statement now the position is clarified and we can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, would you answer that question: Do you contend that there was an international court with jurisdiction over these matters that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not contend that. I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so as a good lawyer you advised your clients that there was no international court that could deal with their complaints?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't tell my clients. I'm saying what the clients were saying. I didn't say that to them. That's what I made clear a moment ago. I didn't mention any international court. I just said that at the time I was aware that there was a human rights court in Strasbourg and I knew that we couldn't go to that court because we were not members of the Council of Europe. I was saying that my clients were saying that, and not myself. Maybe due to my occupation, I wouldn't have to answer this question because this relates to counsel-client privilege but if you insist, I am telling you what I said, but it wouldn't be ethical for me to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, I will not insist that you answer a question, please understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest, Mr. Ackerman, that you proceed with some other point, some other question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to talk to you now about people losing their jobs. You told us that you had clients who had lost their jobs because of decisions made by the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you told us that these clients brought you documents which, on their face, said that they had been dismissed because of an order of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have those documents?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have them with you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did the investigator of the Prosecutor ask you for those documents?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you given them to the investigator for the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, they have not -- I don't think, been disclosed to us and I think it's very important that they be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do know something about this but the situation is, and can I confirm, he did offer them and the investigator rang and we said that we couldn't take them because they weren't his to offer them to us. They [Realtime transcript read in error "we"] were his clients' files and they were confidential so they were never taken, but he certainly did offer them to us and we don't have them. I can confirm that we didn't take them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman. I just want to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Mr. Ackerman. I just want to check something in my records because I have an indication, an impression, that the witness in his statement made some kind of reservation about these documents, saying precisely what Ms. Korner has just -- yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask for the note to be corrected as well? My answer a wasn't "we were his clients' files" but "they were his clients' files."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Any way, we will come to this later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have -- given evidence but I can call the investigator if necessary, if Mr. Ackerman requires to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, in each case, where he mentions even the names of his clients, it does state that he has -- still has in his possession, the original files.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What Your Honour may be thinking about is when I dealt with this matter in examination-in-chief, I asked a series of questions about whether he'd been able to contact any of his clients to obtain their permission for us to have the files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You probably are right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a very moot point and one which we couldn't resolve at the time as to whether or not the clients still retained their rights of privilege in these files, but we decided to be safe rather than sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we proceed for the time being, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your honour, the witness was asked directly, "Did you give these to the investigator for the Prosecutor?" just now, and his answer was "Yes," and what his statement might say is of no moment. What he just said right here in open was he gave them. Secondly, these are documents that were provided to the client by their business, the place they worked. They are not part of any attorney-client privilege. They can't be part of any attorney-client privilege that I'm aware of and if the witness is going to testify that he has documents saying that they lost their job because of an order from the crisis staff, then those documents need to be produced. And I demand that they be produced. I request that they be produced. And if he's correct that the Prosecutor has them, then the Prosecutor should give them to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. I just stated we don't have them. We didn't take them. They were offered to the investigator. I can call the investigator to say that and if Mr. Ackerman requires it, I will. If Mr. Ackerman requires Mr. Dzonlic to have those documents -- produce those documents, well, then, I have no doubt some arrangements can be made or we can try to in Sarajevo, but, Your Honour, we do not have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dzonlic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said, and I was asked by the attorney whether I had those documents, I said that I didn't have them on me but that I do have possession of them, and when I said that I gave the documents, what I meant was that, when I was examined, I said that I had the original documents, and I gave them those documents to look at, but I didn't officially hand over those documents to the Prosecution as evidence, because of the ethics of my job and for other reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we have to stop here for the time being because we have overstepped by five minutes and my attention has been drawn to that fact. We will recommence at 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I apologise? I gather I've kept you waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. [Microphone not activated] Yes. Just one follow-up. Bad news, Mr. Ackerman. I wasn't right when I said we were supposed to resume or we had agreed to resume on April the 4th. The Registry has located the part in the transcript of the session of 21st January, and I'm reported as having said -- I'm the culprit. I take all the responsibility. Okay, so let's go back. We start on the 23rd, break from the 8th until the 13th, recommence on the 14th, right through the 21st, then break from the 22nd, I gave you an extra day now, break from the 22nd until April the 1st, resuming on April the 2nd in any case. I wouldn't have liked to resume on April the 1st because I don't know whether you have taken me seriously. So that is the position. So the agreement is that we will resume on April the 2nd. If you require more time than April the 2nd or you want to resume later than April the 2nd, because of logistics in particular, do let me know and we can -- one day here or one day there wouldn't make a difference because we will make up for it later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to make inquiries today to see whether there is any problem getting the witnesses here because it will mean them coming here on Easter Sunday actually, if not Easter Saturday and it may cause a difficulty, but I will check that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Keep us informed. And if we need to adjust the timetable, you know, taking another couple of days off in that week and then adding another couple of days sitting somewhere else, we can do that. It's a question of -- the important thing is that we go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I correct? I was told this morning that I think all our lists of the numbers of witnesses were -- there was one wrong number, number 8, the witness I said we were going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, let me locate the paper because that, I think, is here. Yes, what is the problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two witnesses with the same name. It's Witness number 8, who in fact does not have the number 7.197 but 7.103, who we are skipping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. No. In my list, witness number 8 is 7.197. And witness number 13 is also 7.197.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And they both have the same name and I would assume that they are the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. They are different. So it's witness number 8 who in fact has the disclosure number of 7.103, who we propose to admit -- omit completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. We will get to know the name later. Obviously for our purposes, I think Mr. Ackerman and Madam Fauveau can follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The first names are different but it's the surnames that are the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The person that you are going to dispose of, in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. other words --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You said you wouldn't require him would be number 13 now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No it's number 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's no longer important for us to know who he is at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid that that happens quite a lot from certain areas, a lot of people have the same name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Number 13 you're going to produce as a witness later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And in fact, I didn't raise the matter up myself. I should have actually because the number was the same. But one has the asterisk and the other one doesn't. So one was seemed to be protected and the other one wasn't. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused now is the order then, Ms. Korner 7, 9, 10, 11?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Ms. Korner, while you are still standing, do I still take it that witness number 19, 7.167, will not be produced?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is so. That was a Rule 92 and in the light of Your Honour's ruling we have taken the decision not to call him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that between 14 and 15, there is an additional witness, number 7.4, correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, Your Honour, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you aware of that, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me see. I've got a 7.4 at place 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I said between 14 and 15 because that's where I marked him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, we updated the list and clearly, Your Honours, and myself are still working off the old list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am. Okay. Thank you, Ms. Korner. I think you can bring forward the witness. Yes, Mr. Dzonlic, again sorry to have kept you waiting but we were discussing a few matters. Mr. Ackerman will continue with his cross-examination of you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, before we broke, you had told us with regard to these documents we were discussing, you know what I'm talking about, don't you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that you showed them to the investigator for the Prosecutor; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have testified about their contents here in this courtroom; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you now take the position that there is some kind of a privilege attached to documents that you have shown to the Prosecutor investigator and talked about here in the courtroom that would prevent you from giving us the documents?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that this is a question of ethics. This is -- this concerns the client-counsel privilege, the client-counsel relation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, didn't your showing them to the Prosecutor's investigator concern the client-counsel privilege relation? Didn't you violate that by showing them to the Prosecutor's investigator?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I showed these documents to them to confirm what I knew, but I didn't present them as an official -- as official proof to the Court, to the Tribunal, and it was not taken as evidence by the Chamber. I really don't have the consent of all my clients to submit these documents and to submit them as official evidence to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman. Let's specify what these documents we're to start with. Because before we start even discussing or putting questions to the witness, whether he violated then or would violate now the confidentiality rules between advocate, counsel, lawyer and client, we better specify what documents we are talking about. What were these documents? What did you show to the interrogating officer at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I showed the investigators documents on, to be specific, the termination of employment, the decision of the Crisis Staff, on mobilisation. My objection or complaint filed against this decision, the decision of the court on determining a sentence, most of the documents were of this kind. And my relation with my clients, I never told anyone about what we had spoken about, and I consider that these documents are public ones. If the Trial Chamber and the Defence wants to obtain these documents it's quite simple. It is possible to carry out an official investigation in the municipal court for misdemeanors in Banja Luka for the period of 1992 and there is certainly about 5.000 such cases and the court dealt exclusively with such cases in that -- during that period. I don't want to enter into the Defence's strategy but I think that the Defence is making it more difficult for itself, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please don't enter into arguments with Defence counsel. Mr. Ackerman here is -- has a task to complete. He is has a responsibility towards his client. He may enter sometimes in confrontation with you. You are a lawyer, you have also been a Judge. You understand that. He's doing his duty. So the Court will protect him in as far as he does not go beyond what his duty is. So please, I think you have answered the question as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned. Mr. Ackerman, can we go ahead?
