Because one of these documents actually, which is P255, which he was shown, and I remember him saying that this was or could have been the type of document that his clients were showing him as being the cause or the basis for the termination of their employment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm prepared to go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because basically there may be one of all the documents that he has mentioned, there may be one, which one could argue with a lot of ifs and buts that could be covered by confidentiality or -- but the rest? Where does confidentiality come in?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm prepared to go forward. I'm going to take your guidance and be more specific with regard to what I'm asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, let me be more specific about the exact documents that I'm asking you about. You said in your testimony that you had clients who lost their jobs because of the decision of the Crisis Staff, and that they brought you documents which presumably were from their employers saying that they had been dismissed because of the decision of the Crisis Staff. Is that the case? Do such documents exist?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such documents do exist, yes. For failure to respond to the mobilisation call and the decisions of the Crisis Staff, according to these decisions, the employment of certain people was terminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do the documents say on their face that the dismissal action was taken because of a decision of the Crisis Staff? That's my question. Not the mobilisation call but the decision of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not because of a decision of the Crisis Staff but because of a failure to respond to the mobilisation call.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you told this Chamber the other day that you had documents showing that clients lost their job because of decisions of the Crisis Staff, you were not correct, were you? That you had documents that would show that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see in what respect I was not correct. I said that because of the decision relating -- concerning the failure to respond to mobilisation, and for this reason, employment -- people were dismissed. Anyone who failed to respond to mobilisation would lose his job. Apart from those who had been assigned war obligation -- work obligations and this had been assigned to people for whom the Crisis Staff had given authorisation to work and for people who had provided this -- a copy of this war plan, they would be assigned work obligations and all the others had to go to the army or to the front. All the others weren't able to go to their jobs and for this reason, their employment was terminated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I interrupt? Because I think Mr. Ackerman has put to the witness that he told the Chamber the other day that you had documents showing that clients lost their jobs because of the decisions of the Crisis Staff. Your Honour, I think one needs to look at what he actually said and Mr. Ackerman can put his exact words to him. I think that would be helpful. Your Honour, it's in the LiveNote. I don't know whether an official transcript has yet been produced, for the 26th of February, on my version it's page 69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you read it out, Ms. Korner, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Your Honour, the question was -- I put to him the document of the Crisis Staff that is Exhibit 255.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the one I mentioned myself earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly, and I said:

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic what were the circumstances in which many of the clients were bringing you a copy of this decision?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People would come to see me because they had been dismissed from their work after this decision and they would bring decisions on terminating their employment in which reference was made to this decision. I told the client each client that if it was possible for the client to provide me with this decision from its company, they should ask their employer to provide them with this decision. They would then go back to their company - I don't know how they obtained this - they didn't all manage to obtain the decision, but quite a few of them brought these decisions to me on the basis of which their employment had been terminated and the grounds for the termination were cited as this decision. And he then explained that he had two or three copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was referring to, the document that was brought by his clients citing the decision of the Crisis Staff as the reason that they had been terminated and then what he goes on to say is he asked if they could find that decision and bring it to them and I think he understands that I'm asking him about the documents the clients brought showing they had been terminated, dismissed because of a decision of the Crisis Staff so I don't think there is any difference between what I'm suggesting and what Ms. Korner just read to you. I'm prepared to move on, Your Honour. Unless Your Honours want to pursue this further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I feel no need to pursue it any further. It's so obvious when a client comes to you telling you his or her lawyer, legal adviser, "I've had my job terminated," what that client can produce is a letter of dismissal or of termination of employment. Then the question arises as what is contained therein, whether there is a specific reference and it seems that the specific reference, according to his testimony before, was to the decision of the -- contained in P255 which I could remember very as being the document that he was referring to throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he's now told you today that that's not the case, that the document that the clients brought him referred to the mobilisation order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course the clients don't bring -- I mean, in my country, the basis is an act of parliament. No client is going to bring you the act of parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the matter is completely confused then at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we better ask Mr. Dzonlic to confirm he actually said that yes, he did get a copy of this of that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, eventually they did bring him this. But what they brought him initially was the letter of dismissal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what I'm talking about. He told you that the letter of dismissal referred to a decision of the Crisis Staff as the basis for the dismissal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he also said that several of them brought him also copies of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not what I'm inquiring about. That has nothing to do with my question. He told you that they brought letters of dismissal, that on their face said the dismissal was because of a decision of the Crisis Staff. That's what I'm asking him about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Made reference to whatever it is, a proclamation or decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, Ms. Korner just read you his testimony and that's what he said. Today now he says "No, that's not what those documents say. They only refer to failure to respond to mobilisation." I've made my point. I don't need to make it any clearer, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, I will let the interpreters finish first. You have presumably followed the exchange and the debate for the last few minutes. Are you in a position to clarify the position to us? What did your clients hand to you, what kind of documents did they hand to you, and in particular, if there was a document expressing the termination of their employment, what did that document normally specify as being the reason for the termination? And also, I will put a direct question to you: Was there a reference in these documents to what was shown to you as document -- Exhibit number P255 being the decision of the Crisis Staff of the ARK region, of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of my clients would bring me decisions on the termination of employment. In some of the decisions, it was quite explicitly stated that this was for failure to respond to mobilisation. And that for these reasons, this person's employment was being terminated. In other decisions, on the termination of employment, it stated that on the basis of the decision of the Crisis Staff on mobilisation and failure to report to one's job for three days, employment was being terminated; That concerned the majority of documents. A few clients brought me a decision which had been signed and had a stamp from the Crisis Staff, a decision of the Crisis Staff, because the Crisis Staff forwarded its decisions to economic agents too. And I have perhaps two or three decisions from the Crisis Staff. They were not the originals but they were photocopies of this decision, paragraph 1, 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's clear enough, Mr. Ackerman. We can proceed with the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it's not clear at all, Your Honour, but I will proceed because you instructed me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's not clear to you, you may put any further question you may like. The Chamber is not stopping you. But can I -- can you tell us what's not clear now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have now, as far as tell, three different versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To me, it has always been clear from the very first time he opened his mouth on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me explain my confusion, Your Honour, and maybe you can clarify it for me. He says, "My clients came into the office and brought me a piece of paper. It was a piece of paper from the place they were employed that said, 'You are hereby dismissed.' And the reason for your dismissal is that you failed to respond to mobilisation." That's fine. I can accept that. But what he told you initially was that on the face of the document it said the reason for dismissal was a decision by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With reference to mobilisation and the failure to respond to the call for mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a question of putting a juxtaposition of one with the other and bringing them together in the same context. This is why he sent them back and asked for a further documents to come forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If there is a document that says that his client was terminated based on a decision of the Crisis Staff, not because of mobilisation, but on a decision of the Crisis Staff, then I would -- I think that document should be produced. Because I suggest to you that I don't think it exists. I think the document that exists is a document that says they were terminated because of failure to respond to mobilisation. The mobilisation was ordered by the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina not the Crisis Staff. If there is a -- if there is a document that says they were terminated because of actions of the Crisis Staff, I think it should be brought here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see your point but we don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You certainly have a valid point but we don't have the documents. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you should order them to produce them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he has them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He says he has them. He claims to have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dzonlic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I just try to add something? Some people would lose their jobs not only because of failure to respond to the mobilisation call but directly as a result of the decision of the Crisis Staff, and if we are to go back a little in time, we will see that at all managerial posts, certain senior positions could be held only by citizens of Serb ethnicity. That was a decision of the Crisis Staff. So that people who held managerial positions would automatically lose their jobs pursuant to this decision, because they were not Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But were there any of such persons amongst your clients? I mean clients that had lost their job not because of failure to respond to the mobilisation call but because they held managerial positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were such clients, yes. Who had held managerial posts and lost their jobs merely because they were not of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My question to you, do you have any objection or reservation in making these documents or some of them available to the Prosecution? Or to this Trial Chamber? Ten years after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have certain documents that I gave the Prosecution to examine. I did not oppose showing them to them. But then the problem of a procedural nature arose. I didn't have permission to offer these documents as evidence. If that is necessary, I can provide it for examination, and I leave it up to the Trial Chamber to rule whether it is my duty and obligation to provide those documents. Of course, I think that we should bear in mind the rules of ethics, but I am at your disposal. I don't know whether I have to do this but if I'm given such instructions I will do so without further ado.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the matter ought to stop there for the time being, Mr. Ackerman. That's his answer. Whether he should be forced to produce the documents or not, I don't think ought to be debated in his presence in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your direct testimony, you talked to us about the Crisis Staff of ARK, and what you told us, and I'm referring to page 2322 of the transcript, you told us that the Crisis Staff was responsible for all segments of life on the territory of Bosanski Krajina, and you were asked to elaborate and you said, "Well, all segments of life means, 'ranging from the economy, information, agriculture, the use of power, electricity, education, culture,' so the Crisis Staff took over all control over all aspects of life."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just ask what day, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would have been the 26th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you stand by that testimony, Mr. Dzonlic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by everything I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff have an office in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was based in Banja Luka but where its office was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you even know if it had an office?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You never saw a Crisis Staff office, did you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You never went to a Crisis Staff office or met anybody at a Crisis Staff office, did you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were employed by the Crisis Staff? Did you ever learn that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear who -- I assume if the Crisis Staff was responsible for all of these segments of life, economy, information, agriculture, power, electricity, education, culture, that there would have been a Crisis Staff minister for each one of these segments of the economy. That's the way it should have been; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had an executive council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the executive council was Mr. Erceg and three other people, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you saying that it's the executive council that was responsible for economy, information, agriculture, power, electricity, education, culture and all aspects of life?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw from the decisions signed by the president of the executive council, as far as I can remember now, that referred to these various segments of life and that he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware of the percentages of Serbs, Croats and Muslims in Banja Luka in 1990, 1991?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that very well. I participated in taking the census in 1981 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the census of 1991 showed what, do you know off the top of your head without looking?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially, when we completed the census for Banja Luka municipality, 98.500 Serbs, 28.700 Bosniaks, 29.500 Croats, and I think 26.000 Yugoslavs and 8.000 others. As far as I am able to remember just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You told us that in the judiciary in Banja Luka, in 1990, 1991, there was one Croat judge; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 1993, until I left the Banja Luka, I remember that there was only one Croat judge left at the municipal court in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm talking about before any people were dismissed, like you testified people were dismissed. Before any dismissals that you testified about, there was only one Croat judge, isn't that what you told us?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't say that there was only one Croat judge. I said that only one had been left, only one judge of Croat ethnicity, that he had not been fired, and that he remained in his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I misunderstood you and I apologise. So before --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before all of this, how many Croat judges were there? I know you probably can't be totally accurate but just your best estimate?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of the total number of judges, there may have been, shall I say, -- well, I don't know. There were several, maybe ten, but I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what the total number of judges were?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the total number of judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us about a commission that you set up that had four members, dealing with human rights, that sort of thing, and you established offices for that commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you give us some sense of how large these offices were that you had established for your commission?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an office in perhaps the oldest town -- building in Banja Luka, an old Bosnian house, the size was five by four metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was just a single room, this office?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just that one, single room.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And I think you told us that you needed to accommodate quite a large number of people who, once they learned about your existence, were coming there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to accommodate them. I didn't say that. I just said that when people learned about the existence of this office, a large number of them would come to the office and as the house had a large yard, then those people would be in the yard. And there was a large walnut tree and wooden benches and they would sit there or stand around there. I don't think I said that we needed to accommodate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I used a word that got translated in such a way that you totally misunderstood me. I didn't mean that you were providing them with housing and clothing and food and things like that. What I meant was that you had to take care of whatever issues these people had come there to discuss with you in this office.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked to us about people losing their jobs, and you told us that when people lost their jobs, were dismissed from their employment, that because the flats that they lived in were owned by the company they had been employed by, they then lost their flats and were left with no choice but to leave the area. Is that what you told us?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber of just one case where someone was forced from their flat, against their will, without being assigned another flat to live in in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one? There were hundreds every cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All I'm asking you to tell us is -- if you can tell us one?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand how I can tell you about one. I know of a case of a person being evicted from his flat without another flat being provided for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us that person's name? You don't have to. I'm not going to make you tell us that person's name but can you tell us that person's name?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If necessary, I will. My father-in-law, not to go any further than that. He is my wife's father. My aunt. There you are. They are my relatives. I wouldn't like to mention clients' names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What company was he employed with?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father-in-law, just before the war, retired. He used to be employed in the Institute for the Construction of Banja Luka, it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So he was not dismissed from his job?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He wasn't dismissed, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question was can you tell me someone who was dismissed from their job that was then forced from their apartment without being assigned another one.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, my aunt's son, my cousin. He was employed in the company called Cajevac, Rudi Cajevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he was dismissed for what reason?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he didn't respond to the mobilisation call, and he couldn't enter the factory and three days later, he was fired, and maybe two months later, he was evicted from his apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did he live in that apartment by himself or did he have a family?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a family.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And was he assigned another apartment to move to?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He had to leave Banja Luka, and he is now living, I think it's in Sweden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't have to tell us where he's living.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you -- I'm going to move to another subject now, about -- you told us that you made several trips to the headquarters of the 1st Krajina Corps to try to get permission to go to Manjaca. You recall that testimony, do you not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And just as a practical matter, how were you getting back and forth from your home to the offices of the 1st Krajina Corps? Were you, walking, bicycling, driving? How were you doing that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On foot. I went on foot. I walked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did you have to go through barricades or checkpoints to get there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You eventually got permission to go to Manjaca and you drove there in a vehicle owned, I think you said, by Ibrahim Makic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Makic have to get some kind of a travel permit to permit him to drive his car to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we all had to given our documents, but Mr. Makic, in addition to a copy of his ID card also had to provide a copy of his traffic licence for his vehicle, and it was on the basis of those documents, I think, that we were given permission to go to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm speaking right now about your first trip there, did you have to go through checkpoints or barricades upon leaving Banja Luka or anywhere along the way?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Referring to your first trip to Manjaca, in Ibrahim Makic's red Kombi, did you have to go through any checkpoints or barricades from the time you left the place you left from in Banja Luka until you got to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't. We didn't have to pass through any checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it that Ibrahim Makic lived in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, yes, he lived in Banja Luka. I think it was in the Vrbanja district. I'm not quite sure, but I think that is where he lived and that is part of Banja Luka so he did live in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And his -- this red Kombi that he had that you talked about, was it a Renault?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was a red Renault. It could have been a Ford Kombi van.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You just don't know?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite old. I think it was a Ford van.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever see him driving it around Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not until that time when we went to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you see him driving it around after that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said that -- you told us that -- actually I'm going to skip some questions here, Your Honour. I think I'll not go into this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This red Kombi, I'm talking now about not the one that Makic drove around but this other red Kombi that you talked about, you told us that that red Kombi was designed to put people in fear and make them want to leave Banja Luka. That was your impression; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was its main purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that people wanted to leave Banja Luka because they didn't want to be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the -- I -- could you please ask me that question once again? I do apologise. Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that people wanted to leave Banja Luka because they didn't want to be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that Serbs left Banja Luka to avoid being mobilised?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Serbs too, who left Banja Luka, and the reason, I don't know their reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if a young Serb was mobilised, he might be sent to fight in the front lines and get killed; right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know, don't you, that Serbs left Banja Luka to avoid being mobilised and sent to the front lines, sons of rich families, primarily?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know some Serbs who left. Whether they were sons of wealthy families, I don't know that, but I do know that individual Serbs left Banja Luka because they didn't agree with the overall situation, and did not want to join the army, to go to war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. And Croatians in Banja Luka didn't want to join the army and fight against other Croatians in Croatia, did they?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They did want to join the army and fight against Croatians or did I misunderstand your answer?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't want to join the JNA and to fight in Croatia against Croats in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you're aware, are you not, that Alija Izetbegovic instructed Muslims not to respond to the mobilisation for the war in Croatia, saying that it was not the Muslims' war and they shouldn't go there and fight? You heard that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. You've perhaps misinterpreted that information. Mr. Alija Izetbegovic on behalf of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina called on all the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not the Muslims, but all the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not to respond to the mobilisation call and not to go to war in Croatia because that was not our war, and he meant the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And it is not right that he called on the Bosniaks. I didn't hear that. And I do know that he called on all the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina not to go to that war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, at the time, Bosnia-Herzegovina was a Republic of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those days, it had already been recognised, that is both Croatia and Slovenia had been recognised. So that the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was no longer that, what it was by name, because Slovenia and Croatia had already acquired their independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But Bosnia-Herzegovina had not. It was still part of the SFRY, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a part of the SFRY but I was saying which SFRY. Not the one that used to include all the former republics, because with the dissolution of Yugoslavia, sovereignty and independence of Slovenia and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Croatia were recognised, so that Bosnia and Herzegovina did not have the same status that it used to have before these two republics' independence was recognised. So that it's a -- it's a fact that Bosnia and Herzegovina was still not independent at the time. That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And during that war that was going on in Croatia, when there was a mobilisation call, like the Croats and the Serbs, the Muslims didn't want to be mobilised and go fight in that war either; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority didn't want to go. The majority didn't want to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Under the laws of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in existence at that time, what were the penalties for failing to respond to a mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, only answer the question if you are in a position to answer it. I know you are a lawyer, but if you're not in a position to answer that question, don't answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't tell you with precision what the penalties were. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. You know there were penalties for failure to respond to the mobilisation call under the laws of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, don't you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know that a lot of people were leaving to avoid being mobilised or being punished for failure to respond to mobilisation, both -- Serbs, Muslims and Croats, all three?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mobilisation applied to all citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, in addition to this red Kombi that you said put people in fear and made them want to leave, you also said that there were other things going on in the Banja Luka area that put people in fear and made them want to leave; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's your position, is it not, that this was a deliberate thing, that the persons in charge, the Serbs, were deliberately trying to create a climate of fear to force people to leave, Muslims and Croats, non-Serbs, to leave Banja Luka and the Krajina area? That's your basic position, is it not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I would like to do with you now, Mr. Dzonlic, is go through the process that was required for you, once you had decided to leave Banja Luka, the process that you had to go through to get permission to leave, and I'd like to go through these kind of one at a time. One of the things you told us that you had to do was go to the police; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't first have to go to the police. You had to go to the police in order to leave. You had to go to the police to deregister, to say you were leaving and to say that you were going to resettle somewhere else and the second place you were going to register in would usually be in some other country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go with first. What was the first place you had to go, first thing you had to do?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there was not a first thing you had to do. It wasn't as if you had to do one thing first. You could first go to the housing organ and get a certificate confirming that you didn't have a certain rights to a flat, and then you could go to get a certificate saying that you had sold something. There was no definite sequence that had been established, but in fact you had to go through the entire procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's just try to go through them one at a time and I think the order, as you said, is not important. When you'd go to the police, the purpose in going to the police was what? What did you have to do when you got there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You had to fill in a form, which -- with which you would register and deregister. Would you have to say that you were leaving, deregistering and you would also have to write down your new place of residence. So you would have to state that you were leaving a certain address on such and such a date, and would you have to state that you were going to be resident at a certain different address on a certain date, and then the competent organs in the police would enter this in your identity card on the third -- on the second or third page of the identity card. They would make a note of the date of deregistration. They would put their stamp on the third page of that identity card then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you were going to move from Banja Luka to Belgrade in 1989, you'd have to do the same thing, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No? You weren't required to go deregister with the police before you left town?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were free to move. I went to Zagreb on 50 occasions. I never deregistered. We never had to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You didn't go there to live there. You went there to visit; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me when you go to Belgrade, so do you mean when you go, when you move to live somewhere else? I didn't understand you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what I meant. That translation, my word choice was probably bad. If you wanted to move from Banja Luka to Belgrade, change your residence, in 1989, you'd have to go through this same process, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the same process.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that you had to go to, I think, National Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what would happen there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were all liable for military service, and we had our military booklets, and a certain records in which our data had been noted, and our mobilisation post as a reservist was stated there. You would have to take your booklet, that booklet there, you would have to take your uniform with you if you had one, you would have to hand over your uniform and hand over that booklet and deregister, deregister with the secretariat, I suppose, and then you would get a certificate stating that you had deregistered with the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, in 1989, if you were going to move from Banja Luka to Sarajevo, you'd have to do the same thing, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The whole idea of this was you were part of a reserve army basically, the TO, and for them to be able to call you up, they had to know where you were. So if you were going to move from Banja Luka to Sarajevo, you had to inform National Defence you were changing your residence, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I really don't know. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would make sense, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not comment on this because I don't know. For registration and deregistration of your place of residence, yes, I'm aware of this, but I don't know about this other issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know if you were emigrating, leaving the country to move to Europe, the United States or somewhere else, that in 1989, you had to go to National Defence, turn in your military identification, your uniform, all those things? You know that was the case, don't you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It Would be sensible, wouldn't it? Doesn't that make sense?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're insisting on an answer but as I said, I don't know. You may or may not accept my answer, but I don't know. Even if someone emigrated, in such a case, that means he might leave without contacting anyone. I don't know. I really can't comment on this because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, please understand that I'll always accept your answer that you don't know. I can't make you know something that you don't know. If you don't know something, just say so. That's just fine. Okay? You told us you would have to go to the court. What would happen there? What would you do at the court?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you went to the court, you had to submit an application to them for a certificate stating that no criminal proceedings were being conducted against you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, when you would do that, would you have to stand in a line? Were there -- was there a whole line of people there trying to get such certificates?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There probably was. I don't know. Probably, because I, as the lawyer for some people, I would get these certificates, I had access to the records of the court, there were people who were waiting in line there, an application would be made, submitted to the municipal court, and the certificate could be obtained from the high court, in another court, so you would submit the application to the municipal court and after two or three days, would you go to the higher court in order to obtain this certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you did it for yourself, didn't you get one of these certificates yourself when you were getting ready to leave?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to get all these certificates too because, as I said, I finally got this authorisation to leave but they then took it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The certificate you got from the court they took away from you? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. The authorisation to leave, to resettle. But all of these certificates that I received from the courts and from all other institutions, they would be returned to them again in some other office, maybe it's a matter of 14 or 15 certificates, and we then had to return all of these, pay 50 marks in order to receive one certificate for resettlement, for moving away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you went to the court to get your certificate, the one that you got for yourself when you were getting ready to move away, did you have to stand in line there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never waited in the court, as an ordinary client. As a lawyer I was able to enter without waiting, and to submit certain applications. This was the court records where lawyers could go. There were people who would record things there and as lawyers we were able to enter freely. That was related to our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In 1989, if you were applying for a passport, you'd have to go to the court to get this certificate, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a passport, I'm not sure whether for a passport or for an identity card. Perhaps for a passport it was necessary to have a certificate showing that you hadn't been sentenced and that no criminal proceedings were being conducted against you. I think that this certificate was necessary when a passport was being issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And what you had to pay -- you said you paid 50 marks but wasn't it 50 dinars?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 50 marks. 50 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many dinars would that be?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Believe me. I didn't say that I paid 50 marks for this certificate from the Court. I paid a certain tax, court tax. I don't know how much it was exactly. I gave 50 marks. That was an office. When we would collect all these documents, we would go to that office which was across the road from -- when you crossed the city town in Banja Luka, where there was a building of the local commune. This is where we would provide -- where we would hand in all the documents we had collected and we would pay 50 marks and would then receive a certificate stating that we had paid 50 marks. They would take all those documents and would then issue one document, an authorisation -- which would be the authorisation for moving away. And I paid 50 marks on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that in addition to the police, national defence and the court, you also had to go to various public offices. What were those public offices you had to go to?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You had to take from the cadastre office, the land registry office, which was in the municipality of Banja Luka, your certificate of property, which showed whether you had property or not. And then you had to go to get -- to the title deeds office, which was part of the municipal court, and you with would have to get a certificate of -- on property, if you owned real estate, or you would receive a certificate showing that you were not the owner of real estate on the basis of the records in the -- on land -- of the land registry. You would then have to go to the post office to obtain a certificate showing that you weren't a telephone subscriber, or that if you were, that you were cancelling your telephone subscription. And then you would have to go to the water supply board and the sewer board - I think that's what the firm was called - in order to obtain a certificate stating that your supply system was being cancelled, and that the refuse collection was being cancelled. You would then have to go to the fund -- the resources management in the municipality of Banja Luka in order to obtain a decision stating that you didn't owe any taxes or that you weren't liable for taxes, or that if you were, that you had paid all your taxes. Then you would have to go to the housing organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I have to stop you and I have to stop the witness because now he's repeating almost verbatim when he has already told us before. You were proceeding in an orderly manner, asking him particular questions in relation to each particular visit that he was supposed to make before he could resettle elsewhere. Could you please go ahead as you were proceeding before, if you still need to do that, without having the witness to go over and over again, repeating what he has already told us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, all these public offices that you had to go to to get all these certificates was something you would have to do in 1989 if you were moving from Banja Luka to Belgrade, isn't it? You would have to disconnect your water, you would have to disconnect your sewer, you'd have to get a certificate that you didn't owe any money, you'd have to disconnect your telephone, you'd have to do all these things, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because I don't know anyone who moved. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you told us, when you first testified about this -- you're now saying you don't know. You told us, when you first testified about this, that this process where you had to go through, the police, the national defence and the court and all these public offices, was set up by the Crisis Staff. That's what you said. Now you're telling us you don't know.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify this a little? You were speaking very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your testimony to this Trial Chamber a day or two ago, you said that this process that you've described, going to the police, the national defence, the court, and all these public offices, was set up by the Crisis Staff. Now you're saying you don't even know. What's the truth?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the entire procedure had been established after a decision by the Crisis Staff on the manner of leaving, and on issuing certificates. Before, such procedure did not exist, if someone wanted to leave. You have just asked me whether all this was in 1989, whether it was the same in 1989. I don't know whether it was the same in 1989 but all I do know is that you first had to deregister, to say that you were leaving your place of residence, and I know that at that time the people did not have to go through that procedure when they had to leave. And furthermore, earlier on, when you wanted to leave, you didn't have to obtain a certificate, an authorisation to leave. You were free to leave. But as identity cards were public documents, you had to regulate this matter, but you did not have to receive some sort of particular authorisation to leave because you wanted to leave. That's what I was saying and that's what I was thinking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, do you understand that what you're saying is being recorded in a transcript? You understand that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you just told us over the last ten or 15 minutes was that before the war, in 1989, you had to go to the police and go through this same process to move. You knew that to be true. With regard to the National Defence, you said you didn't know. With regard to the courts, you said you didn't know, but you knew you had to do it to get a passport. With regard to all these various public offices, I asked you if you had to do it before and you said you didn't know. You had told the Court, you had told this Tribunal under oath that this was a process that was set up by the Crisis Staff, that the crisis staff said you had to go to the police and the National Defence and the court and the cadastre office and all these other public offices. What I'm saying to you, and what I suggest to you, is that you did not tell the Chamber the truth when you told them that, because you've just now told us that you had to do it before or you don't know that you had to do it before. Now, what is it? What's the truth?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that I said is true. You can claim whatever you like. What I said, I stand by what I said. And as far as I can remember, this was also a decision of the Crisis Staff on issuing certain certificates. We were all -- in order to leave Banja Luka, we all had to go through this procedure in order to obtain permission to leave. That's what it was called. Officially it was called a certificate for leaving and the people called it permission to leave. We had to go through all of this in order to obtain this permission to leave. And it was only then that we would be allowed to leave. And I stand by what I said. I don't see that I said anything else, anything other than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where is this decision from the Crisis Staff you're talking Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about? Have you seen it since you've been here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where is this decision from the Crisis Staff that you talk about? Have you seen it since you've been here, the one that required you to do all these things?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was yesterday or the day before yesterday, that at that point in time the Prosecutor asked me whether I was referring to those certificates, when I was speaking about the certificates. And the decision of the Crisis Staff -- there was a decision of the Crisis Staff on issuing certificates for departure and certificates on the property owned by citizens, and I said that I was referring to those certificates. I -- at the moment, I don't know about other decisions and whether -- perhaps you too -- whether you too were aware of these decisions. You were following the proceedings. I confirm that I was referring to those certificates because each citizen had to receive a certificate permitting him to leave. There must have been people who left illegally without those certificates. But whoever wanted to leave in accordance with this had to go through such a procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I understand what you're saying now is that you had to have a certificate to permit to you leave. And I understand that. That's not what I'm asking you about. What you told us was that this process you described -- you went in great length in your testimony describing the process that you were going through again today and the judge stopped you. You said that entire process was set up by the Crisis Staff. And what I'm asking you is, is there a decision of the Crisis Staff that you have seen since you've been here that says you have to go to the police and the National Defence and the court and the cadastre office and all these other public offices and get certificates from all those offices. Is there a such a decision of the Crisis Staff and if so, have you seen it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that there was a decision of the Crisis Staff on that but that there was a decision of the Crisis Staff stating that you had to receive such a certificate. But as far as this procedure is concerned, I didn't say that there was a decision of the Crisis Staff saying -- listing a number of items that had to be done. I said that on the basis of the Crisis Staff's decision it was necessary to obtain certificates to leave and a certificate on property in order to be able to take your property out, you had to go through -- I'm not quite sure what kind of procedure relating to property, but you had to get this certificate for permitting you to leave. And in order to obtain this certificate, you had to go through this entire procedure and only at that point would you receive such a certificate permitting you to leave. And I said that earlier on, it was not necessary to have a certificate permitting to you leave, and that this procedure did not exist, because no one needed a certificate if someone wanted to leave on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With that, I think we have to break for the next 25 minutes. We will resume at 5 to 1.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before the witness comes in, could I just mention the timetable again? I've consulted with the investigator responsible for arrangements with the VWS who bring witnesses here. It's thought that possibly the last witness for the Banja Luka municipality may still be actually giving evidence after the Easter break because we are going back and back again, but if not, and to be on the safe side whereas I'm asked to ask you if you could, say, split the difference and make it the 3rd of April which is the Wednesday rather than the Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Knowing that if I remember well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm saying this subject to correction, but it may well be that on that particular -- on that Friday on that particular week, may be court maintenance. I have the impression that it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We worked on the basis it's court maintenance, no sitting on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Good. So the understanding is, Madam Fauveau and Mr. Ackerman, that we will be resuming on the 3rd and not on the 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm having trouble with LiveNote. Yes. I understand I think what Ms. Korner said, we will not sit on the 22nd and we will not sit again until the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, your better half will have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Put up with me for an extra day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She won't be angry with you about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When I say your better half, I mean it. Can we call the witness, please? Thank you. She is not a lawyer, too, is she?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She is as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, she is. She works for the government, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least she doesn't work pro. Bono

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dzonlic, we will continue with your cross-examination. Mr. Ackerman, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, the last answer that you gave us regarding these tasks that one had to do before leaving Banja Luka, your last answer was, "I didn't say that there was a decision of the Crisis Staff on that. But there was a decision of the Crisis Staff stating that you had to receive such a certificate." In your testimony on February 27th, starting at page 2398, Ms. Korner, you had been talking about the -- all these things you had to do, this list that you and I went through this morning, and Ms. Korner said to you, "You said a that departure from Banja Luka was clearly established and orchestrated by the authorities. Why do you say that?" Then another question right after that. "You say you knew the authorities arranged it. How do you know that?" And then up a fairly long answer, about departure and all the things that one had to go through, and you talk about electricity bills, heating bills, power distribution centre, the public institutions, the court, the Defence Secretariat, your answer goes through that whole list you and I were talking about. And then Ms. Korner says in question,

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm going to stop you for a moment. I think before we go any further, was this something that always happened? In other words, before these events in 1992, or was this something that had only happened as a result of the Crisis Staff and the like?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the result of decisions of the Crisis Staff. Before that, it never happened. Now, that was your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, can I interrupt? Mr. Ackerman has the same facility I do, it's 2389, if Your Honour is looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've got 2398.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed. Mr. Dzonlic,

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was your testimony, Mr. Dzonlic, at whatever page it appears. Now, do you want to take back what you told us before the break that you didn't say there was a decision of the Crisis Staff on that? That you had to go through all this process?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not taking it back. I said that before, we didn't have this procedure for permission to move, which all of us had to go through. Before the war, there was no such procedure for someone to leave his own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think the transcript will speak for itself, Mr. Dzonlic, I don't think it's of any value for me to proceed any further with you on that. This Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region, you saw the documents showing who the members of the Crisis Staff were. We looked at several of them here yesterday or the day before. You recall that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you'd agree with me, wouldn't you, that in addition to the listed names, it's pretty clear that the Crisis Staff would also have included representatives from the other municipalities that were part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that because I don't know all the people on the list of the Crisis Staff. Those that I do know are from Banja Luka. As for the others, I don't know where they are from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's kind of my point. The municipalities outside Banja Luka wouldn't have for a minute put up with a Crisis Staff that was only people from Banja Luka, would they?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm sorry, I object to that question. How can he say what people from other municipalities would have put up with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if he doesn't know he's free to say, I've already told him, that he can say he doesn't know any time he feels like it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: ... is a valid one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask it differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You rephrase it, it's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether representatives from all these other municipalities that were part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina would have consented to a Crisis Staff that was made up of all people from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, it's a question which I wouldn't expect him to answer in any case. How can he answer for others?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm just asking him if he knows. Maybe he does. If you don't want him to answer the question, that's fine with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you aware of what Mr. Ackerman is asking you, as a fact? Or as a possible fact? Because it's also a hypothetical situation that he is putting to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware that it is an assumption and I can answer in the form of an assumption. I assume that the Crisis Staff was composed of representatives of the whole territory, and that probably all the members of the Crisis Staff were not from Banja Luka municipality alone, that is my assumption. I don't know that. I just do know the people that I knew and whom I have identified, they were from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could I ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P242? Well, that is not anywhere near the document that I thought it was going to be. Apparently we have an exhibit numbering problem, Your Honour. And it's obviously my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: According to my records, at least to my binder, 242 is a copy of a draft translation of a decision by the Serbian -- by the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff to found an agency for population movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it's 247 is the one I'm looking for. I think it's 247. I've got a 242A and a 247B. I think it's probably 247. The disclosure is 2.64.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzonlic, you have before you Prosecution Exhibit 247, and the B/C/S version is 247B. This is a -- refers to a meeting of an organisation apparently called Intermunicipal Agreement Sanska Unska [phoen] area of 14 June, 1992, with representatives from Srpska Krupa, Bosanski Petrovac, Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Dubica, Prijedor, and Sanski Most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you look at paragraph 1, just below the listing of the agenda you'll find language in B/C/S had starts with [No interpretation]. In English it reads, "With regard to the previous meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, we can note that most of our proposals have been adopted and have been incorporated into the official positions of the Crisis Staff taken at its 8 June, 1992 session." That at least indicates, does it not, that your assumption is correct, that there were people from these other municipalities in attendance at and making proposals at this meeting of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this document for the first time. However, this first item, since it is of a general nature, the first paragraph doesn't specify what it is they discussed, and what proposals they made that were incorporated in the positions of the Crisis Staff. So I don't know what this relates to. Therefore, I don't understand fully what really you are asking me, what it is you want. Perhaps you could elaborate a little and explain it to me better.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll try again. All I'm really asking you, I think, is something that's fairly simple. The question I'm asking you is: That document indicates, does it not, in paragraph 1, that representatives from these municipalities listed up above were present and making proposals at that Crisis Staff meeting on 8 June? I'm not interested in what those proposals were, just that it tends to support your assumption that people from other municipalities were members of the Crisis Staff. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could make such an inference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I'm asking. Thank you. I'd like you to keep that document because we will be referring to it again and I'd now like you to be provided with P227. You looked at this document at some length yesterday and had reviewed it prior to your testimony here; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the first decision, number 1, is the decision regarding mobilisation, is it not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that decision is signed by Lieutenant Colonel Milorad Sajic, Secretary of the National Defence Secretariat of the Autonomous Region of Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Has nothing to do with the ARK Crisis Staff, does it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that so explicitly, that it has nothing to do with the Crisis Staff of the Krajina region, because here there is reference to the Autonomous Region of Krajina, so it applies to that region as an Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But the Crisis Staff wasn't even appointed until the day after this decision was entered. This decision was entered on 4 May and the Crisis Staff wasn't appointed until the next day, 5 May; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. That's true. But it applies to the Autonomous Region of Krajina, the whole region.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that but what you have referred to as the mobilisation order of the Crisis Staff was not the mobilisation order of the Crisis Staff, it was the mobilisation order of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, because the Crisis Staff didn't even exist when that decision was made. That's a fair statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. One could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it would be correct to say so, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And like some other decisions that you and I have looked at, this one has a preamble, does it not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that preamble says that the decision is being made pursuant to the decision of the Ministry of the National Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, number 1/92, dated 16 April, 1992. That's what it refers to as the authority for it being made; right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you said that this mobilisation was ordered by the municipal secretaries of defence, it's really not true, is it? It was ordered by the Ministry of National Defence and Lieutenant Colonel Milorad Sajic on behalf of ARK simply followed that order from the Ministry of National Defence of SRBiH; right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in the territory of Banja Luka municipality, the call-up papers for the general mobilisation, the general call-up and individual call-up papers were distributed by the municipal Secretariat for National Defence of Banja Luka municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you seen the document referred to, the decision of the Ministry of National Defence of SRBiH of 16 April, 1992? Have you ever seen that document?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one I'm looking at now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, the one from the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. number 1/92, the document that the one you're looking at now refers to. Have you ever seen that document?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen that document. I can't remember. Maybe if I were to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit 153, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have it before you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, if that is the one. 1/92?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the one referred to in Sajic's decision; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this decision in Prosecutor's Exhibit 153 declares an imminent threat of war, in paragraph 1, under the second decision. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the second paragraph in that decision, general public mobilisation of the TO, in the entire territory of SRBiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And finally all military conscripts are duty-bound to make themselves available to the municipal TO staffs in the territory of SBiH -- SRBiH maybe, I don't know. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, go back now to the Official Gazette and the decision of Lieutenant Colonel Sajic.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what Lieutenant Colonel Sajic is ordering in this decision is a mobilisation of the Territorial Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to number 2, the Crisis Staff according to this document, was 17 people, and they were all appointed to their position by Nikola Erceg; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who you know to have been the president of the executive council of the Autonomous Region of Krajina at that point?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the Crisis Staff would be available to replace the ARK Assembly if it was not possible for the ARK Assembly to meet. That would be the purpose of the Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Didn't you say that in your statement to the OTP, that the purpose of the Crisis Staff was to take the place of the assembly when the assembly couldn't meet? Do you want to deny that you said that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I said that the executive council --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt. I think in this case the witness should not be asked to remember his statement. It should be put to him and let him look at the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me just look, Your Honour, and make certain that my memory is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your memory is correct because I remember him making this statement. But there was a previous occasion when in fact you were suggesting to him that he had said this and that and when you could have read it out to him, and I would suggest to you that this should be adopted as the practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it helps Mr. Ackerman, it's in his second statement at the top of page 5, the paragraph that he may be thinking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you actually say at the place where -- you don't even have it in front of you. I think you should. It's his second statement, dated May 5, 2001. It would be fair for to you have it rather than me telling you what it says. Just look at the top of -- it might not be page 5 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Under a heading called "Crisis Staffs." It's on page 4 at the very bottom of the page, "Krisni Stab," and the first paragraph, [no interpretation]. Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you say in there, that "the Crisis Staff is the organ that would make decisions that were once made by a municipal assembly, for example Serb Krajina Assembly, in Banja Luka municipal government," correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that some of the decisions were taken by the Crisis Staff instead of the municipal assembly, when it was constituted and when it was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you look down into the next paragraph, near the bottom, what you say in your statement is, "The ARK Crisis Staff made the decision for general mobilisation order." And we've just discovered that that's not true, haven't we? That it was -- that was done before there was an ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
